turn.text:
Kleinkünstler, a 42501 on a plain `SELECT` is the building refusing you at the door, not the fridge rules. Bureaucracy does at least sort its refusals by department.

Postgres runs two checks. Grants decide whether a role may run the operation on the table at all. Policies decide which rows the operation applies to. A missing grant raises `42501` before any policy runs [1]. A `USING` clause that filters rows out raises nothing and returns zero rows [2]. For a `SELECT`, an error means the grant layer (or schema access), not your policy. Note that a `WITH CHECK` violation on a write also raises 42501, but your statement is a read.

Caveat: `lab_control` says lab `01-rls-vs-grant` isn't the active lab, so I haven't seen your table. Replace `public.your_table` below with the real name. Run this and paste the result:

```sql
select
  has_schema_privilege('authenticated', 'public', 'usage')              as schema_usage,
  has_table_privilege('authenticated', 'public.your_table', 'select')  as table_select;
```

Expected: either value can be `false`. The error text also says which one failed, "permission denied for schema" or "for table". Say "show me" if you want the full fix later.

Given that `42501` on a `SELECT` points at the grant layer, which of the two columns do you expect to come back `false`?
